questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Negating one whole clause with a single word
questions.learningObjective: negate a whole clause with one negative word and place it correctly
questions.stem: A Spanish speaker wants to say that nobody opened the window. Which sentence makes that claim using one negative word and no other?

options.text: 'No ventana la abrió', with the negative word placed after the subject and before the verb as a set phrase
options.misconception: believes the negative word may sit anywhere before the verb, even between the subject and the object

options.text: 'Nadie abrió la ventana', with the negative word standing in front of the verb and nothing else negated in the clause
'No abrió nadie la ventana', which carries two negative words and so makes the claim twice over
options.misconception: believes that a second negative word makes a negation emphatic rather than reversing it into a double negative

options.text: 'Nadie no abrió la ventana', with the two negative words placed on either side of the verb as a way of stressing it
options.misconception: believes two negative words in one clause can be stacked as emphasis, which reverses the single claim

questions.explanation: A Spanish clause takes one negative word. 'Nadie' is a pronoun that stands for the subject, so it goes in the subject slot and the verb agrees with the third person singular: nadie abrió. Nothing else in the clause is negated, and the sentence says exactly what the English sentence says. The version with a negative word on both sides of the verb is the one a learner writes when a language class has told them that a double negative means a strong yes, and in Spanish it does the opposite: 'nadie no abrió' asks whether it is not the case that nobody opened it, so it leaves open that everybody did. The version carrying two copies of the plain negative has the same fault, and the version with the negative word inside the verb phrase is a different error again, since the negative word belongs before the verb and cannot be pushed in after the subject.
questions.hint: Ask how many negative words the clause allows, and where the subject slot is.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Where the word no sits in a Spanish clause
questions.learningObjective: place the negative word in front of the verb of a Spanish clause
questions.stem: A learner wants to say that they did not arrive on time and writes the negative word after the object. Where does the negative word belong?

options.text: Attached to the subject rather than to the verb, so the sentence reads 'no nosotros llegamos a tiempo' and only the subject is denied
options.misconception: believes the negative word can qualify the subject, so that the people are denied and the arrival is not

options.text: In front of the verb, so the sentence reads 'no llegamos a tiempo' rather than 'llegamos no a tiempo'
Between the verb and whatever follows it, so the sentence reads 'llegamos no a tiempo'
options.misconception: believes the negative word splits the verb from its own complement

options.text: At the very end of the sentence, so the sentence reads 'a tiempo no llegamos'
options.misconception: believes the negative word belongs after the whole clause as an afterthought

questions.explanation: The negative word goes in front of the verb, and the verb governs whatever follows it: no llegamos a tiempo. The preposition a and the phrase it introduces are bound to llegar, so pushing the negative word between them pulls the verb's complement apart. The version that puts the negative word at the very end produces a clause that is hard to parse, because a phrase brought in by a preposition cannot be stranded at the end of a clause while the verb stays in front of it. The version that attaches the negative word to the subject has a second fault as well as the wrong position, because a negative word so placed denies the people rather than the arriving, so a speaker reading 'no nosotros llegamos' takes the denial to be about who is arriving and hears no claim at all about whether they arrived on time.
questions.hint: Ask which word the negative word has to sit in front of, and what that word brings with it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Answering a positive question with a negative one
questions.learningObjective: answer a positive question with a negative that denies only part of it
questions.stem: Someone asks in Spanish whether the shop is open today and the speaker wants to say that it is open but not on a Sunday. Which answer says that?

options.text: 'No, porque no es domingo', which denies the opening and then gives a reason that has nothing to do with the hours
options.misconception: denies the opening outright and attaches a reason that does not account for it

options.text: 'Sí, pero no el domingo', which agrees with the question and then denies one single case
'No, no está abierta', which denies the whole question and so says the shop is shut today as well
options.misconception: reads the answer as denying the opening altogether, so the qualification about Sunday is lost

options.text: 'No está abierta el domingo', which denies the opening on Sunday and says nothing about the rest of the week
options.misconception: puts the denial on the one day that is meant to be excepted and leaves the general claim untouched

questions.explanation: A negative answer to a positive question is a full denial, so if the shop is open today the answer cannot begin with a bare no. The way to agree and then narrow is to say sí and then introduce the exception with pero: 'sí, pero no el domingo'. The version that puts the denial on the Sunday alone is the near miss a learner writes, and it says something different, because denying the Sunday opening leaves the answer to the question that was asked completely unanswered. That is why the exception needs an opening clause to hang from. The version that denies the opening outright and then supplies a reason fails twice over: the bare no at the front denies the opening, and the reason it offers would in any case not explain a shop being shut.
questions.hint: Ask whether the first word denies the whole question or only one part of it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Adding a second negative with tampoco
questions.learningObjective: add a second negative to a clause that is already negative
questions.stem: A speaker has already said that they did not go to the meeting and wants to add that they did not telephone either. Which wording adds the second denial?

options.text: 'Llamé no', with the added negative word closing the clause after the verb
options.misconception: believes the added negative word may be moved to the end without changing the claim

options.text: 'Tampoco llamé', with the added negative word carrying its own verb form and following the first denial
'No llamé tampoco', with the added negative word placed at the end of the clause as a set phrase
options.misconception: believes the added negative word is a fixed ending that belongs after the whole clause

options.text: 'No no llamé', with a second copy of the same negative word in front of the verb
options.misconception: believes a second copy of the negative word is the way to add a further denial in Spanish

questions.explanation: A clause in Spanish takes one negative word, so a second denial is made with a different word rather than a second no. 'Tampoco' means not either and it stands on its own: it comes with a verb of its own, in this case llamé, and the two denials sit side by side, 'no fui a la reunión, tampoco llamé'. The version that puts the word at the end of the clause, where the prepositional content of the first denial already is, and the result is not a form a speaker produces. The version carrying two copies of the plain negative is the double negative that a language class warns about, and in Spanish the two copies of no cancel rather than combine, so it points the other way. The version that closes the clause with the word is the same error with the word moved.
questions.hint: Ask which word Spanish uses when a second denial is added to a negative clause.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The correlative pair ni and ni
questions.learningObjective: join two negative alternatives with the correlative pair
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say that a person is neither a doctor nor a teacher. Which sentence states that, with the two alternatives joined the Spanish way?

options.text: 'No es médico o profesor', with the ordinary conjunction joining the two alternatives inside one negation
options.misconception: uses a conjunction that can mean or as though it joined the alternatives inside a single negation

options.text: 'No es médico ni profesor', with the negative word outside and the correlative repeated before each alternative
'No es ni médico ni profesor', with the correlative placed in front of the verb as well as before each alternative
options.misconception: repeats the correlative one time too many, so the two alternatives are governed by two separate negatives

options.text: 'Ni es médico ni profesor', with the correlative standing where the verb would otherwise go
options.misconception: believes the correlative can replace the verb rather than join the two alternatives

questions.explanation: Two negative alternatives take the correlative ni in front of each one, and one negative word governs the pair: no es médico ni profesor. The form with the negative word outside and the correlative before each alternative is the one built the way the language builds it. The version that puts the correlative in front of the verb as well is the near miss, because a learner who has just learnt that a correlative comes in pairs expects the pair to begin at the verb, and the extra copy makes the verb look like one of the two alternatives. The version that lets the correlative stand where the verb belongs leaves the clause without a verb, since the correlative is not a verb and cannot stand in that slot. The version that uses the ordinary conjunction is the error a speaker of English makes, where not a doctor or a teacher is ambiguous in the same way, and the difference between o and ni is exactly the difference between a disjunction and a coordinated negation.
questions.hint: Ask how many times the correlative appears and where the single negative word goes.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The indefinite negative words for nothing and for nobody
questions.learningObjective: use the indefinite negative words in the slot each one occupies
questions.stem: Two English sentences say that a person said nothing and that nobody spoke. Which pair of Spanish sentences puts each negative word in the slot its meaning requires?

options.text: 'Nada no dijo' and 'no habló nada', with each negative word standing in the slot belonging to the other one
options.misconception: swaps the two negative words, so each is put in a slot its meaning does not fit

options.text: 'No dijo nadie' and 'nada no habló', with the subject word used as an object and the object word used as a subject
options.misconception: puts each indefinite negative word in the slot meant for the other one

options.text: 'No dijo nada' and 'no habló nadie', with one word as the object and the other standing in for the subject
'No dijo nada' and 'nadie no habló', with the subject word repeated in front of the verb in the second sentence
options.misconception: repeats the negative in front of the verb as though a second word strengthened it

questions.explanation: Nada and nadie are not interchangeable, because each has its own slot. 'Nada' is an object, so it goes where the thing that is not there would have gone: no dijo nada. 'Nadie' stands in for the subject, so the verb is third person singular and the sentence is no habló nadie, with nadie allowed in front of the verb or set after it for emphasis. A learner who has met the two words in a list often treats them as a pair of synonyms and swaps them, which produces a sentence that is grammatical and says something else, and that is the failure the two versions that swap the words are built on. The version that repeats the negative in front of the verb is the double negative again, and the two copies of no cancel each other instead of reinforcing.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two words stands for the subject and which is the object.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The negative time adverb and where it sits in the clause
questions.learningObjective: place a negative or emphatic time adverb against the verb of a clause
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say in Spanish that they have never been to that city. Which sentence says it, with the time adverb in the right place?

options.text: 'Nunca estoy en esa ciudad', with the present tense, which says the person is not there now
options.misconception: reads a statement about the whole of a life as a statement about one moment in it

options.text: 'No estoy nunca en esa ciudad', with a second negative word in front of the adverb as well
options.misconception: stacks a second negative word in front of the negative adverb and so cancels the claim

options.text: 'Nunca he estado en esa ciudad', with the adverb in front of the verb phrase and the verb in the perfect
'He estado nunca en esa ciudad', with the adverb closing the clause after the verb phrase
options.misconception: believes the negative time adverb may be moved to the end of the clause as a set ending

questions.explanation: Nunca belongs in front of the verb phrase, and the tense carries the rest: nunca he estado says that at no point up to now has the person been there, which is what never does in English. The choice of the perfect is what makes the claim about a life rather than about a moment, and that is what the version in the present loses, because no estoy nunca says the person is not there at the moment of speaking and leaves the rest of the life unclaimed. The version that puts the adverb at the end strands it where the prepositional content of the sentence already sits, and the clause stops parsing. The version that adds a second negative in front of the adverb, and the two cancel, so it no longer denies anything at all.
questions.hint: Ask which tense carries a claim about a whole life, and where the adverb sits.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The word ningun and the noun it has to agree with
questions.learningObjective: make the negative determiner agree with the noun it stands in front of
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say that there were no classes yesterday. Which phrase gets the determiner, the noun and the verb to agree with one another?

options.text: 'Ningún clases hubo ayer', with the determiner moved after the noun and the verb in front of it
options.misconception: believes the negative determiner can follow the noun it belongs to

options.text: 'Ningún clase no hubo ayer', with the determiner in front of the noun and a second negative word in front of the verb
options.misconception: stacks a second negative word in front of the verb, which cancels the first claim

options.text: 'No hubo clases ayer', with the negative adverb carrying the denial and the plural noun left as it stands
'No hubo ninguna clase ayer', with the negative determiner in front of a singular noun and a singular verb
options.misconception: believes that making a noun singular after the negative determiner also makes the verb singular

questions.explanation: There are two ways to deny the existence of the classes and only one of them needs agreement. 'No hubo clases' uses the negative adverb with the verb and leaves the plural noun alone, which is the shorter and more common form. The determiner 'ningún' is available as well, and when it is used it must agree with the noun: ningún clase, singular noun, singular verb. The version that keeps the singular noun with the plural verb is the trap, because a learner who has just learned that the determiner changes to the feminine form in front of a feminine noun reaches for that rule here and writes ningún clase while keeping the plural verb that went with the plural noun. The version that moves the determiner after the noun puts it where the verb used to be, and the version with a second negative in front of the verb adds a word that cancels the first, so the sentence ends up claiming that there was a class.
questions.hint: Ask whether the determiner or the adverb does the denying, and what has to agree with what.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Sin with a gerund and sin with an infinitive
questions.learningObjective: use the preposition of absence with either a gerund or an infinitive
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say that she left without paying and, in another sentence, that she left without saying goodbye. Which pair of clauses uses the preposition correctly in each?

options.text: 'Salió no pagando' and 'salió no despidiéndose', where the preposition has been replaced by the negative adverb
options.misconception: believes a gerund can be negated directly without a preposition to carry the absence

options.text: 'Salió sin pago' and 'salió sin despedida', where both complements are nouns naming the missing thing
options.misconception: turns both complements into nouns and loses the action each one was supposed to leave out

options.text: 'Salió sin pagar' and 'salió sin despedirse', where the first takes a gerund and the second an infinitive
'Salió sin pagó' and 'salió sin decir adiós', where the first takes a past form and the second an infinitive
options.misconception: believes the preposition of absence can take any verb form, including a past one

questions.explanation: Sin governs the action that did not happen, and the action can be given either as a gerund or as an infinitive. 'Sin pagar' leaves out an action the subject was doing, and 'sin despedirse' leaves out an action the subject ought to have done; both are the same construction with two different forms of the verb, and a speaker chooses between them by what is meant, not by a rule about the verb. The version that puts a past form after the preposition gives it something no Spanish verb does. The version that replaces the preposition with the negative word is the error that comes from a language whose gerund needs no preposition, because the gerund here is not a verb form standing on its own but a noun phrase headed by sin. The version that makes both complements nouns leaves out the doing rather than the not doing.
questions.hint: Ask which forms the preposition accepts, and what each one leaves out.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: No with a verb of knowing, wanting or being able to
questions.learningObjective: negate a whole infinitival clause through the verb that governs it
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say that they cannot come, and in another sentence that they do not want to come. Which pair of sentences carries the negation on the right verb?

options.text: 'No poder venir' and 'no querer venir', where the negation has been pushed onto the infinitive itself
options.misconception: believes a verb of ability or wanting can carry an infinitive with a negative word of its own

options.text: 'No puedo no venir' and 'no no quiero venir', where a second negative word is placed in front of the infinitive
options.misconception: stacks a second negative word on the infinitive and so reverses the whole claim

options.text: 'No puedo venir' and 'no quiero venir', where the negative word stands in front of the verb of ability and the verb of wanting
'No vine no puedo' and 'no quiero no venir', where the negative word is repeated in front of the second verb as well
options.misconception: repeats the negative word in front of each of the two verbs and so cancels the claim

questions.explanation: A whole infinitival clause is negated by putting the negative word in front of the verb that introduces it, not in front of the infinitive. Saber, poder, querer and deber all introduce an infinitive and all take the negative word themselves: no puedo venir denies the ability, no quiero venir denies the wanting, and the infinitive that follows is left unmarked. The version that puts the negative word on the infinitive is the error a speaker of English makes, since 'cannot come' keeps the negation on the main verb and the learner transfers the habit. Both versions that add a second negative word are making the same error, and in Spanish the two cancel, so 'no puedo no venir' says the opposite of what was meant, which is that the person has to come.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two verbs is the one the negative word belongs to.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Nada de before an infinitive and the phrase that means only
questions.learningObjective: use the phrase for nothing but in front of an infinitive
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say that a person does nothing but wait. Which sentence says that, and which phrase does the work?

options.text: 'No hace nada de esperar', with the preposition form of nothing but taking the infinitive after it
options.misconception: believes the preposition de governs an infinitive in this construction, which it cannot in Spanish

options.text: 'No hace nada más', with the verb left out so the phrase has nothing to restrict
options.misconception: leaves the verb out and so produces a fragment rather than a sentence

options.text: 'No hace nada más espero', with the infinitive replaced by a first person form of the same verb
options.misconception: turns the infinitive into a finite form and so makes the phrase govern a second clause

options.text: 'No hace nada más que esperar', with the phrase for nothing but taking the infinitive after it

questions.explanation: The phrase that means nothing but is 'nada más que', and it introduces an infinitive: no hace nada más que esperar. The three parts have separate jobs and each can be got wrong. 'Nada más' on its own means only, and it is a different expression that needs something to restrict; the version that leaves the verb out drops it and leaves a fragment. 'Nada de' is a real form, but the de governs a noun, as in no hace nada de ruido, and it does not govern an infinitive, so the version using the preposition form is not a form a speaker produces. The version that replaces the infinitive with a finite verb, which turns the phrase into the start of a new clause and changes the claim from a restriction to a statement of what the person does.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two forms takes an infinitive and which takes a noun.

questions.topic: Negating an existential statement with no hay
questions.learningObjective: negate the existence of something in Spanish
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say that there is no lift in the building. Which sentence says that, with the negative word on the verb that states existence?

options.text: 'El edificio no tiene ascensor', which puts the negative word on a verb of holding rather than of existence
options.misconception: puts the negative on a verb of possession and so changes the shape of the claim from existence to holding

options.text: 'No es ascensor el edificio', which uses the verb of being in place of the verb that states existence
options.misconception: believes the negative word can sit on the verb of being and say the same thing

options.text: 'No hay no ascensor', which adds a second negative word in front of the noun for the lift
options.misconception: stacks a second negative in front of the noun and so cancels the denial

options.text: 'No hay ascensor en el edificio', with the negative adverb in front of the verb that states there is

questions.explanation: Spanish has a verb for stating that something exists, and the negative word goes in front of it: no hay. The version that uses the verb of holding is also a correct sentence and says something different, since tener says the building holds a lift rather than that a lift is there in it, and the two claims come apart in the case of a building that has a lift in a part of it that the speaker did not see. That is why the existence verb is the one to reach for when the claim is about there being one at all. The version that puts the negative on the verb of being leans on a verb that cannot state existence and says only that the building is not a lift. The version that adds a second negative in front of the noun cancels the two, and the sentence then leaves open that there is a lift.
questions.hint: Ask which verb states that something exists at all, and put the negative in front of it.

questions.topic: The phrase that means only and rules out a second one

options.misconception: uses two words for nothing in the same phrase and so doubles what should be one restriction

options.text: 'No hace otra cosa no trabajar', which adds a second negative word after the noun phrase
options.misconception: adds a second negative word and so cancels the restriction entirely

questions.topic: Putting a negative adverb before the verb or after it
questions.learningObjective: use the word that means never in either of its two positions

options.misconception: believes a second copy of the negative adverb strengthens a claim already made

options.text: 'No habla' and 'habla no', which place the negative word on either side of the verb in the same order
options.misconception: believes a plain negative word can be moved past the verb and still negate the clause

options.text: 'Nunca no habla' and 'no habla nunca', which add a second negative word in the first and not in the second

options.text: 'Nunca habla' and 'no habla nunca', with the adverb in front of the verb in one and after it in the other

questions.topic: Ser and estar with a negative predicate
questions.learningObjective: choose between the two verbs of being for a negative description of a broken thing

'La bicicleta no es funcionando', which puts the infinitive straight after the first verb of being
options.misconception: believes the first verb of being can govern an infinitive in this position

options.text: 'La bicicleta no está para funcionando', which inserts a preposition before the infinitive without a purpose
options.misconception: believes a preposition of imminence can be left in front of an infinitive with no further verb

options.misconception: believes the first verb of being can take a noun made out of a verb in this slot

questions.topic: Negating a time clause with hasta que and mientras
questions.learningObjective: negate a subordinate time clause and keep the main clause's tense
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say that a person will not leave until somebody arrives. Which sentence says that, and what does its main clause use?

options.text: 'No se irá hasta que llegue alguien', with the negative word in the main clause and the second verb in the right mood
'No se irá hasta que llega alguien', which uses an indicative in the clause of time instead of the required mood
options.misconception: believes the clause after hasta que takes the same tense as the main clause

options.text: 'No irá hasta que llegue alguien', which leaves out the pronoun that carries the object of the main verb
options.misconception: drops the pronoun and so removes the object of the verb of going

options.text: 'No se irá hasta que alguien llegar', with the second clause left without a finite verb of its own
options.misconception: leaves the second clause without a finite verb, so the subject stands where the verb belongs

questions.explanation: The negative word goes in the main clause, and the clause of time after hasta que takes the mood the language uses there, which is the one that reports the event as not yet realised. questions.stem: Stage one: rewrite the four sentences in the stimulus so that each carries one negative word and nothing else. Stage two: for each change, name the rule that decided it.

answer.exemplar: Stage one, the four corrected sentences: no quiero ir. Nunca he estado en esa ciudad. No es ni médico ni profesor. No tengo ganas de trabajar. Stage two, the rule behind each change. The first sentence has two faults and they are both about position: the negative word belongs in front of the verb of wanting, so no quiero rather than quiero no, and the infinitive it governs takes no negative word of its own, so the second no goes as well. The second sentence keeps its adverb meaning never, which is one of the two words that may stand on either side of the verb, and the no in front of the verb has to go, because a second negative word in the same clause cancels the first and the sentence then claims the opposite. The third sentence already has its single negative word in front of the verb of being and its correlative in front of each of the two alternatives, so the word standing at the end is an extra and nothing is left for it to do. The fourth sentence has a negative word in front of the verb and a second one in front of the noun, and the second is the one to remove, because the noun after the verb is not itself what is being denied. The single question behind all four is how many negative words the clause contains, and a learner who asks it will not need a different rule for each sentence, which is what the second stage is testing.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The verb of owing as an obligation and as a likelihood
questions.learningObjective: keep apart the two senses of the verb of owing and the preposition that marks them
questions.stem: Explain to a learner how Spanish keeps apart an obligation and a likelihood, and say which form each one takes in front of an infinitive.

answer.exemplar: The two senses are carried by the same verb, and what separates them is what follows it. 'Debo terminar el informe' is an obligation: the speaker is saying the report has to be finished, and the sentence makes no claim about how likely that is. 'Debo de terminar el informe' is a report of likelihood: the speaker is saying the report looks as though it will be finished, and the person the sentence is about may never be told. The preposition is the only difference, it has to be there for the likelihood sense, and the bare form will not carry it. The same pair works in the past, where the likelihood takes the preposition as well and is the reading a speaker usually intends by 'debía de ser'. Negation is where the difference is easiest to hear, since a bare 'no debe' denies the obligation and is a stronger statement than the speaker may have meant, while a negated form with the preposition denies only the likelihood. A learner who treats the two as one verb will either make promises nobody made or report a guess as a duty, and those two errors change what a listener does next, which is why the preposition is worth learning for this verb alone.

questions.explanation: A verb with two senses that differ only by a preposition is worth explaining as a pair rather than as a list, because a learner who has it as two items will not know which one to reach for. The way to decide is to ask what the speaker is committing to. An obligation commits the speaker, and the sentence is about what has to happen; a likelihood commits the speaker to nothing, and the sentence is about what appears to be happening, with the person it concerns not necessarily involved at all. The second half of the explanation is where the pair earns its place: negation makes the difference audible, because a negated obligation says the thing is not required at all while a negated likelihood says only that it does not look required, and those are different claims with different consequences. The past works the same way, which is worth mentioning because the likelihood reading is the one speakers usually intend in the past.
questions.hint: Ask what the speaker is committing to, and what a negated form of each one denies.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Choosing the right frame for four clauses
questions.learningObjective: repair four verb frames and name the rule behind each repair

stimulus.kind: four clauses typed by a learner
stimulus.body: Puede a venir mañana. Tengo que de llamar. Acabo a salir. Hay que iré.
stimulus.license: Original text written for this item by the author; no third-party text is reproduced.

questions.stem: Stage one: rewrite the four clauses in the stimulus so that each frame has the shape it takes. Stage two: name the rule that decided each change.

answer.exemplar: Stage one, the four repaired clauses: puede venir mañana, tengo que llamar, acabo de salir, y hay que ir. Stage two, the rule behind each. The first two share one rule: a frame built on a modal verb, or on the verb of having, takes its infinitive directly, and nothing comes between the frame and the infinitive, so the preposition in each of them has to go. The third uses a different rule, because the preposition here is not a leftover but a substitution: this frame is built on the verb of finishing and it requires the preposition that ties it to the infinitive, so the error is not an extra word but the wrong one, and the preposition in front of another verb is a different frame with a different sense. The fourth is about what a frame can take: a frame of obligation takes an infinitive, and a finite verb of the future is not an infinitive, so the ending has to come off. The single question behind the first two is whether anything may stand between a frame and its infinitive, and the answer is that nothing may; the other two are about a particular frame's preposition and about the grammatical form the frame requires, and a learner who has only learned the first rule will repair the fourth clause by swapping the verb instead of taking the ending off.

questions.explanation: Four clauses, three rules, and the two rules that are the same are deliberately placed at the ends so that a learner has to notice the difference. The frames of ability and of having are one unit with the infinitive that follows them, and the preposition in each clause is a word imported from a different construction; a learner who has seen a preposition between a verb and an infinitive elsewhere in the language will carry the habit over. The third clause is the opposite case, where the frame needs its preposition and the learner has put a different one there, so the repair is a substitution rather than a deletion, and a response that treats all four as deletions will get it wrong. The fourth clause is about grammatical form rather than about prepositions at all, since the frame of obligation wants an infinitive and a future form is not one. Naming the three rules separately is the second stage, and it is the part that carries: a set of four repaired clauses with no rules attached will be undone again by the next set of four.
questions.hint: Ask for each frame what it takes after it, and whether the preposition is extra or missing.
